entries.passageText: Seek not that the things which happen should happen as you wish; but wish the things which happen to be as they are, and you will have a tranquil flow of life.
entries.reflection: Much distress comes from insisting that events match our wishes. Epictetus suggests the reverse: accept what happens and act well within it. This is not passivity; it frees your energy for the things you can actually do.
studyPrompts: What are you wishing were different right now?
What part of the situation is within your control?
How might accepting what has happened free you to act better?

entries.passageText: The art of life is more like the wrestler's art than the dancer's, in respect of this, that it should stand ready and firm to meet onsets which are sudden and unexpected.
entries.reflection: Marcus compares life to wrestling rather than dancing: it is less about a graceful routine and more about being ready when you are suddenly grabbed. Courage, in this sense, is readiness. What you practise on quiet days is what holds when things change fast.
studyPrompts: What sudden challenge have you faced recently?
What habits help you stay ready for the unexpected?
What could you practise now that would help you on a hard day?

entries.passageText: There are more things, Lucilius, likely to frighten us than there are to crush us; we suffer more often in imagination than in reality. I am not speaking with you in the Stoic strain but in my milder style. For it is our Stoic fashion to speak of all those things, which provoke cries and groans, as unimportant and beneath notice; but you and I must drop such great-sounding words, although, Heaven knows, they are true enough. What I advise you to do is, not to be unhappy before the crisis comes; since it may be that the dangers before which you paled as if they were threatening you, will never come upon you; they certainly have not yet come.
entries.reflection: Seneca notices how much suffering happens in anticipation. Many feared things never arrive, and those that do are rarely as large as imagined. Deal with today's real problems, and let tomorrow's arrive before you meet them.
studyPrompts: What are you dreading that has not happened yet?
How much of your stress today is about real events and how much is about imagined ones?
What would it look like to meet today's problems only?

entries.passageText: Do the things external which fall upon thee distract thee? Give thyself time to learn something new and good, and cease to be whirled around. But then thou must also avoid being carried about the other way; for those too are triflers who have wearied themselves in life by their activity, and yet have no object to which to direct every movement, and, in a word, all their thoughts.
entries.reflection: Marcus warns against two kinds of restlessness: being pulled around by outside events, and frantic busyness without purpose. Real rest comes from having a clear aim. Pause long enough to ask what today's effort is actually for.
studyPrompts: What is pulling your attention in too many directions?
What is the clear aim behind your work today?
When could you take time to 'learn something new and good'?

entries.passageText: When thou wishest to delight thyself, think of the virtues of those who live with thee; for instance, the activity of one, and the modesty of another, and the liberality of a third, and some other good quality of a fourth. For nothing delights so much as the examples of the virtues, when they are exhibited in the morals of those who live with us and present themselves in abundance, as far as is possible. Wherefore we must keep them before us.
entries.reflection: Marcus recommends a simple practice: when you need cheering up, think of the good qualities of the people around you. In a unit, those people are close at hand. Noticing their strengths is both gratitude and encouragement.
studyPrompts: Name a strength you see in three people around you.
Have you told any of them what you appreciate?
How does noticing others' virtues change your own mood?

entries.passageText: Let not future things disturb thee, for thou wilt come to them, if it shall be necessary, having with thee the same reason which now thou usest for present things.
entries.reflection: Anxiety about the future assumes we will face it unequipped. Marcus points out that we will bring to it the same reason and judgment we use today. You have handled hard things before, and you will bring that ability with you.
studyPrompts: What future event worries you most?
What abilities have helped you through past difficulties?
How can you strengthen your judgment today for whatever comes?

entries.passageText: Nothing happens to any man which he is not formed by nature to bear. The same things happen to another, and either because he does not see that they have happened, or because he would show a great spirit, he is firm and remains unharmed. It is a shame then that ignorance and conceit should be stronger than wisdom.
entries.reflection: Marcus holds that nothing happens to a person that they are not formed by nature to bear. He notes that others endure the same things, sometimes out of pride or simply not noticing. If they can, reasoned resolve can as well.
studyPrompts: What are you enduring right now that feels like too much?
Who have you seen carry something similar?
What would 'remaining unharmed' look like for you in this situation?

entries.passageText: When a man has done thee any wrong, immediately consider with what opinion about good or evil he has done wrong. For when thou hast seen this, thou wilt pity him, and wilt neither wonder nor be angry. For either thou thyself thinkest the same thing to be good that he does, or another thing of the same kind. It is thy duty then to pardon him. But if thou dost not think such things to be good or evil, thou wilt more readily be well disposed to him who is in error.
entries.reflection: When wronged, Marcus asks first: what did this person think was good? Understanding the mistake turns anger into something closer to pity, and pardon follows. This does not excuse harm, but it keeps someone else's error from ruling your mind.
studyPrompts: Who has wronged you recently?
What might they have believed was good or right when they acted?
How would pardoning them change your own state of mind?

entries.passageText: No longer talk at all about the kind of man that a good man ought to be, but be such.
entries.reflection: Marcus is impatient with endless talk about virtue. The point is to be good, not to describe goodness. One honest action today says more than any discussion of character.
studyPrompts: Where is there a gap between what you say you value and what you do?
What is one concrete good action you can take today?
Who in your life models integrity without talking about it?

entries.passageText: I thank you for writing to me so often; for you are revealing your real self to me in the only way you can. I never receive a letter from you without being in your company forthwith. If the pictures of our absent friends are pleasing to us, though they only refresh the memory and lighten our longing by a solace that is unreal and unsubstantial, how much more pleasant is a letter, which brings us real traces, real evidences, of an absent friend! For that which is sweetest when we meet face to face is afforded by the impress of a friend’s hand upon his letter,—recognition.
entries.reflection: Separated from his friend, Seneca finds that letters bring the friend near, carrying real traces of the person. For anyone far from home, a message is more than information; it is a kind of presence. Write to someone today, or reread something from someone you miss.
studyPrompts: Who do you miss most right now?
What message or letter from someone has meant a lot to you?
Who could you write to today?

entries.passageText: Let us see to it that the recollection of those whom we have lost becomes a pleasant memory to us. No man reverts with pleasure to any subject which he will not be able to reflect upon without pain. So too it cannot but be that the names of those whom we have loved and lost come back to us with a sort of sting; but there is a pleasure even in this sting.
entries.reflection: Seneca writes to a friend grieving a loss. He hopes that memory of the dead will become pleasant in time, while admitting it still stings. Grief and gratitude for a life can sit together.
studyPrompts: Who are you missing right now?
What memory of them brings you comfort?
How might the sting of grief become something you can carry?

entries.passageText: Remember that thou art an actor in a play, of such a kind as the teacher (author) may choose; if short, of a short one; if long, of a long one: if he wishes you to act the part of a poor man, see that you act the part naturally; if the part of a lame man, of a magistrate, of a private person, (do the same). For this is your duty, to act well the part that is given to you; but to select the part, belongs to another.
entries.reflection: Epictetus compares life to a play: you do not choose your role, but you can play it well. Duty is doing the part you have been given as fully as you can. Choosing the role is not always in your power; playing it is.
studyPrompts: What role are you playing right now?
What would playing it well look like today?
What part of your situation is not yours to choose?

entries.passageText: You may hold converse with your friends when they are absent, and indeed as often as you wish and for as long as you wish. For we enjoy this, the greatest of pleasures, all the more when we are absent from one another. For the presence of friends makes us fastidious; and because we can at any time talk or sit together, when once we have parted we give not a thought to those whom we have just beheld.
entries.reflection: Seneca suggests that friends can be present in thought when apart, and that absence can even sharpen how we value them. This does not erase the ache of distance. It does mean the connection is not lost.
studyPrompts: Who are you apart from right now?
How do you keep them present in your thoughts?
What could you write or say to them?

entries.passageText: Receive [wealth or prosperity] without arrogance; and be ready to let it go.
entries.reflection: Marcus advises receiving good fortune without arrogance and being ready to let it go. Humility here is holding success lightly. What comes can go, and our worth is not in it.
studyPrompts: What success or advantage do you currently enjoy?
Could you let it go if you had to?
What does holding things lightly look like for you?

entries.passageText: On the occasion of every accident (event) that befalls you, remember to turn to yourself and inquire what power you have for turning it to use. If you see a fair man or a fair woman, you will find that the power to resist is temperance (continence). If labor (pain) be presented to you, you will find that it is endurance. If it be abusive words, you will find it to be patience. And if you have been thus formed to the (proper) habit, the appearances will not carry you along with them.
entries.reflection: Epictetus says every difficulty is a chance to use a power you already have: endurance for pain, patience for insults. Hard moments become training. You are better equipped than you think.
studyPrompts: What difficulty are you facing right now?
What power do you have to meet it?
How could you turn this into practice?

entries.passageText: If a man is mistaken, instruct him kindly and show him his error. But if thou art not able, blame thyself, or blame not even thyself.
entries.reflection: Marcus suggests that when someone is mistaken, we should show them kindly. And if we cannot, we should not make it worse with blame. Kindness keeps the door open.
studyPrompts: Who around you is mistaken about something?
How could you correct them kindly?
When has someone corrected you kindly?

entries.passageText: Everything exists for some end,--a horse, a vine. Why dost thou wonder? Even the sun will say, I am for some purpose, and the rest of the gods will say the same. For what purpose then art thou,--to enjoy pleasure? See if common sense allows this.
entries.reflection: Marcus notes that everything exists for some purpose, and asks what his own is. It is not merely to enjoy pleasure. Asking the question honestly is a start.
studyPrompts: What do you believe your purpose is?
What gives your days meaning?
How does your current work connect to your purpose?

entries.passageText: When thou hast been compelled by circumstances to be disturbed in a manner, quickly return to thyself, and do not continue out of tune longer than the compulsion lasts; for thou wilt have more mastery over the harmony by continually recurring to it.
entries.reflection: Marcus advises that when you are thrown off balance, you should return to yourself as soon as you can. Homecoming, and the adjustment it can bring, may unsettle you. Return to your steady self, again and again.
studyPrompts: What has thrown you off balance recently?
What helps you return to yourself?
What will help you adjust when you come home?

entries.passageText: Remember that it is not he who reviles you or strikes you, who insults you, but it is your opinion about these things as being insulting. When then a man irritates you, you must know that it is your own opinion which has irritated you. Therefore especially try not to be carried away by the appearance. For if you once gain time and delay, you will more easily master yourself.
entries.reflection: Epictetus says it is not the insult that harms you but your judgement about it. He also gives practical advice: take time before reacting. Delay gives reason a chance to catch up.
studyPrompts: What has irritated you recently?
What judgement did you make about it?
How could you build in a pause before reacting?

entries.passageText: But if you consider any man a friend whom you do not trust as you trust yourself, you are mightily mistaken and you do not sufficiently understand what true friendship means. Indeed, I would have you discuss everything with a friend; but first of all discuss the man himself. When friendship is settled, you must trust; before friendship is formed, you must pass judgment. Those persons indeed put last first and confound their duties, who, violating the rules of Theophrastus, judge a man after they have made him their friend, instead of making him their friend after they have judged him. Ponder for a long time whether you shall admit a given person to your friendship; but when you have decided to admit him, welcome him with all your heart and soul. Speak as boldly with him as with yourself.
entries.reflection: Seneca says to judge carefully before you call someone a friend, but once you do, trust them fully. Trust is built on judgement, then given without reservation. That is how close teams work.
studyPrompts: Who do you trust fully, and why?
How do you decide who to trust?
Is there someone you hold back from trusting?

entries.passageText: Adapt thyself to the things with which thy lot has been cast: and the men among whom thou hast received thy portion, love them, but do it truly [sincerely].
entries.reflection: Marcus urges you to accept the circumstances you have been given, and to love the people you share them with, sincerely. You did not choose your unit, but you can choose how you treat them.
studyPrompts: Who are the people you have been placed among?
How could you show them genuine care?
What makes it hard to love those around you?

entries.passageText: Remember that the ruling faculty is invincible, when self-collected it is satisfied with itself, if it does nothing which it does not choose to do, even if it resist from mere obstinacy. What then will it be when it forms a judgment about anything aided by reason and deliberately? Therefore the mind which is free from passions is a citadel, for man has nothing more secure to which he can fly for refuge and for the future be inexpugnable. He then who has not seen this is an ignorant man; but he who has seen it and does not fly to this refuge is unhappy.
entries.reflection: Marcus calls the mind free of passions a citadel, a secure place to which we can retreat. Self-control is not suppression; it is having somewhere steady to stand. It can be built over time.
studyPrompts: What disturbs your inner calm most?
What helps you return to your citadel?
How can you practise self-control today?

entries.passageText: Love the art, poor as it may be, which thou hast learned, and be content with it; and pass through the rest of life like one who has intrusted to the gods with his whole soul all that he has, making thyself neither the tyrant nor the slave of any man.
entries.reflection: Marcus advises loving and being content with the craft you have learned, however modest. Contentment comes from valuing your own skill and work. It frees you from envy.
studyPrompts: What skill or craft have you learned?
How do you feel about your work?
What would being content with it look like?

entries.passageText: If thou art able, correct by teaching those who do wrong; but if thou canst not, remember that indulgence is given to thee for this purpose. And the gods, too, are indulgent to such persons; and for some purposes they even help them to get health, wealth, reputation; so kind they are. And it is in thy power also; or say, who hinders thee?
entries.reflection: Marcus says that if you cannot correct someone who does wrong, remember that forbearance is given to you for this. Mercy is a power we can choose to use. It is always within reach.
studyPrompts: Who has wronged you recently?
Could you correct them, or is forbearance better?
When has someone shown you forbearance?

entries.passageText: If any man is able to convince me and show me that I do not think or act right, I will gladly change; for I seek the truth, by which no man was ever injured. But he is injured who abides in his error and ignorance.
entries.reflection: Marcus says he would gladly change if shown he is wrong, because no one was ever harmed by the truth. Honesty starts with being honest with yourself. Being open to correction is part of it.
studyPrompts: When were you last shown you were wrong?
How did you respond?
Is there a truth you have been avoiding?

entries.passageText: Do not disturb thyself by thinking of the whole of thy life. Let not thy thoughts at once embrace all the various troubles which thou mayest expect to befall thee: but on every occasion ask thyself, What is there in this which is intolerable and past bearing? for thou wilt be ashamed to confess. In the next place remember that neither the future nor the past pains thee, but only the present. But this is reduced to a very little, if thou only circumscribest it, and chidest thy mind if it is unable to hold out against even this.
entries.reflection: Marcus advises not to picture all your future troubles at once, but to deal with the present, which is small and bearable. Uncertainty grows when we imagine everything together. Take it one piece at a time.
studyPrompts: What future troubles are you picturing?
What is in front of you right now?
Is this present moment bearable?

entries.passageText: When thou hast done a good act and another has received it, why dost thou still look for a third thing besides these, as fools do, either to have the reputation of having done a good act or to obtain a return?
entries.reflection: Marcus asks why, after doing good, we look for a third thing: recognition or a return. Generosity is complete in the act. Looking for thanks spoils it.
studyPrompts: When have you helped someone and wanted recognition?
What would giving without expecting look like?
What good act can you do today?

entries.passageText: I do not wish to involve myself in too large a question, and to discuss the treatment of slaves, towards whom we Romans are excessively haughty, cruel, and insulting. But this is the kernel of my advice: Treat your inferiors as you would be treated by your betters. And as often as you reflect how much power you have over a slave, remember that your master has just as much power over you.
entries.reflection: Seneca's advice about the treatment of slaves applies to anyone with power over others: treat those under you as you would want to be treated by those above you. He spoke within a society built on slavery, which his words criticise only in part. The principle still holds for leaders today.
studyPrompts: Who do you have authority over?
How do you want those above you to treat you?
What would it look like to treat your people that way?

entries.passageText: Have I done something for the general interest? Well then, I have had my reward. Let this always be present to thy mind, and never stop [doing such good].
entries.reflection: Marcus says that doing something for the common good is its own reward. Service does not need a payment. Remembering this keeps service from becoming a transaction.
studyPrompts: What have you done for the common good recently?
How does it feel to serve without reward?
What can you do for others today?

entries.passageText: Consider that everything is opinion, and opinion is in thy power. Take away then, when thou choosest, thy opinion, and like a mariner who has doubled the promontory, thou wilt find calm, everything stable, and a waveless bay.
entries.reflection: Marcus says everything is opinion, and opinion is in your power. Change your opinion and you find calm, like a sailor rounding a headland into a still bay. Wisdom begins in how we see things.
studyPrompts: What opinion is causing you distress?
Could you see it another way?
Who helps you see things clearly?

entries.passageText: He often acts unjustly who does not do a certain thing; not only he who does a certain thing.
entries.reflection: Marcus notes that injustice can come from not acting, not only from acting. Failing to do what is right is also a wrong. Justice sometimes requires stepping in.
studyPrompts: Where have you stayed silent when you should have spoken?
What action does fairness ask of you?
What makes stepping in hard?

entries.passageText: Do not act as if thou wert going to live ten thousand years. Death hangs over thee. While thou livest, while it is in thy power, be good.
entries.reflection: Marcus reminds himself that death is near, so be good while you can. This is not meant to frighten but to focus. The time to do good is now.
studyPrompts: How does thinking about death affect you?
What good do you want to do while you can?
What are you putting off?

entries.passageText: I feel, my dear Lucilius, that I am being not only reformed, but transformed. I do not yet, however, assure myself, or indulge the hope, that there are no elements left in me which need to be changed. Of course there are many that should be made more compact, or made thinner, or be brought into greater prominence. And indeed this very fact is proof that my spirit is altered into something better,—that it can see its own faults, of which it was previously ignorant. In certain cases sick men are congratulated because they themselves have perceived that they are sick.
entries.reflection: Seneca writes that he is being not only reformed but transformed, and that seeing your own faults is a sign of progress. Renewal starts with honest awareness. Noticing your faults is not failure; it is growth.
studyPrompts: What fault have you recently noticed in yourself?
How might that awareness be a sign of growth?
What would you like to be transformed in you?

entries.passageText: Occupy thyself with few things, says the philosopher, if thou wouldst be tranquil.--But consider if it would not be better to say, Do what is necessary, and whatever the reason of the animal which is naturally social requires, and as it requires. For this brings not only the tranquillity which comes from doing well, but also that which comes from doing few things. For the greatest part of what we say and do being unnecessary, if a man takes this away, he will have more leisure and less uneasiness. Accordingly, on every occasion a man should ask himself, Is this one of the unnecessary things? Now a man should take away not only unnecessary acts, but also unnecessary thoughts, for thus superfluous acts will not follow after.
entries.reflection: Marcus suggests doing only what is necessary, both in actions and in thoughts. Stillness comes from cutting the unnecessary. Ask: is this one of the unnecessary things?
studyPrompts: What unnecessary things fill your day?
What unnecessary thoughts could you let go?
Where could you find more stillness?

entries.passageText: For thus it is, men of Athens, in truth: wherever a man has placed himself thinking it the best place for him, or has been placed by a commander, there in my opinion he ought to stay and to abide the hazard, taking nothing into the reckoning, either death or anything else, before the baseness [of deserting his post].
entries.reflection: Marcus quotes Socrates: wherever a man has been placed by a commander, there he should stay and face the danger. Steadfastness means holding your position when it is hard. Many in service know exactly what that asks.
studyPrompts: Where are you being asked to hold your position?
What helps you stay steady under pressure?
What does steadfastness cost you?

entries.passageText: It is peculiar to man to love even those who do wrong. And this happens, if when they do wrong it occurs to thee that they are kinsmen, and that they do wrong through ignorance and unintentionally, and that soon both of you will die; and above all, that the wrong-doer has done thee no harm, for he has not made thy ruling faculty worse than it was before.
entries.reflection: Marcus says it is human to love even those who do wrong, remembering they are kin, act from ignorance, and will die as we will. Compassion grows when we see our shared humanity.
studyPrompts: Who is hard for you to feel compassion for?
What do you share with them?
How could you show compassion today?

entries.passageText: Look within. Within is the fountain of good, and it will ever bubble up, if thou wilt ever dig.
entries.reflection: Look within, Marcus writes; there is a spring of good there, if you keep digging. Reflection is not only finding faults; it is finding the good in yourself to draw on.
studyPrompts: What good do you find when you look within?
How do you make time for reflection?
What would you like to dig deeper into?

entries.passageText: Above all, my dear Lucilius, make this your business: learn how to feel joy. Do you think that I am now robbing you of many pleasures when I try to do away with the gifts of chance, when I counsel the avoidance of hope, the sweetest thing that gladdens our hearts? Quite the contrary; I do not wish you ever to be deprived of gladness. I would have it born in your house; and it is born there, if only it be inside of you. Other objects of cheer do not fill a man’s bosom; they merely smooth his brow and are inconstant,—unless perhaps you believe that he who laughs has joy. The very soul must be happy and confident, lifted above every circumstance.
entries.reflection: Seneca urges his friend to learn how to feel joy, real joy that comes from inside rather than from external things. That kind of joy is steady. It does not vanish when circumstances change.
studyPrompts: Where does your joy come from?
What external joys do you rely on?
How could you build a more lasting joy?

entries.passageText: Men are disturbed not by the things which happen, but by the opinions about the things; for example, death is nothing terrible, for if it were it would have seemed so to Socrates; for the opinion about death that it is terrible, is the terrible thing. When then we are impeded, or disturbed, or grieved, let us never blame others, but ourselves—that is, our opinions. It is the act of an ill-instructed man to blame others for his own bad condition; it is the act of one who has begun to be instructed, to lay the blame on himself; and of one whose instruction is completed, neither to blame another, nor himself.
entries.reflection: Epictetus says we are disturbed by our judgements, not by events. The educated person stops blaming others. Responsibility starts with owning how you respond.
studyPrompts: What disturbed you recently?
What judgement did you make about it?
Who do you tend to blame?

entries.passageText: Is any man afraid of change? Why, what can take place without change? What then is more pleasing or more suitable to the universal nature? And canst thou take a bath unless the wood undergoes a change? and canst thou be nourished, unless the food undergoes a change? And can anything else that is useful be accomplished without change? Dost thou not see then that for thyself also to change is just the same, and equally necessary for the universal nature?
entries.reflection: Marcus asks whether anyone is afraid of change, since nothing useful happens without it. Change is the way of nature, and of ourselves. Fearing it is like fearing breathing.
studyPrompts: What change are you facing or fearing?
What good has come from past changes?
How could you approach this change differently?

entries.passageText: Be not ashamed to be helped; for it is thy business to do thy duty like a soldier in the assault on a town. How then, if being lame thou canst not mount up on the battlements alone, but with the help of another it is possible?
entries.reflection: Marcus says not to be ashamed to be helped. A soldier who cannot climb the wall alone still does his duty with help from another. Needing help is not failure; refusing it can be.
studyPrompts: Where do you need help right now?
What stops you from asking?
Who could you help today?

entries.passageText: For what purpose, then, do I make a man my friend? In order to have someone for whom I may die, whom I may follow into exile, against whose death I may stake my own life, and pay the pledge, too. The friendship which you portray is a bargain and not a friendship; it regards convenience only, and looks to the results.
entries.reflection: Seneca says a true friend is someone you would follow into exile or die for, not someone you keep for convenience. Loyalty is the heart of real friendship. It is tested when things get hard.
studyPrompts: Who would you follow into hardship?
Who has been loyal to you?
Is any friendship of yours based only on convenience?

entries.passageText: It is precisely in times of immunity from care that the soul should toughen itself beforehand for occasions of greater stress, and it is while Fortune is kind that it should fortify itself against her violence. In days of peace the soldier performs manœuvres, throws up earthworks with no enemy in sight, and wearies himself by gratuitous toil, in order that he may be equal to unavoidable toil. If you would not have a man flinch when the crisis comes, train him before it comes. Such is the course which those men have followed who, in their imitation of poverty, have every month come almost to want, that they might never recoil from what they had so often rehearsed.
entries.reflection: Seneca uses the soldier who drills in peacetime to make his point: train before the crisis. Discipline in easy times prepares you for hard ones. That is the purpose of drills and exercises.
studyPrompts: What are you training for?
What discipline could you practise now?
How has past training prepared you?

entries.passageText: Accustom thyself to attend carefully to what is said by another, and as much as it is possible, be in the speaker's mind.
entries.reflection: Marcus advises paying close attention to what others say and trying to enter the speaker's mind. Listening is understanding, not just hearing. It is a skill that can be practised.
studyPrompts: Who did you last really listen to?
What gets in the way of your listening?
How could you practise listening today?

entries.passageText: Every soul, the philosopher says, is involuntarily deprived of truth; consequently in the same way it is deprived of justice and temperance and benevolence and everything of the kind. It is most necessary to bear this constantly in mind, for thus thou wilt be more gentle towards all.
entries.reflection: Marcus notes that people go wrong unwillingly, through ignorance, and that keeping this in mind makes us gentler with everyone. Gentleness comes from understanding. It is a choice to see others clearly.
studyPrompts: Who could you be gentler with?
What might they not understand?
How has understanding someone made you gentler?

entries.passageText: So then, to keep up my figure, Fortune has often in the past got the upper hand of you, and yet you have not surrendered, but have leaped up and stood your ground still more eagerly. For manliness gains much strength by being challenged; nevertheless, if you approve, allow me to offer some additional safeguards by which you may fortify yourself.
entries.reflection: Seneca tells Lucilius that fortune has often knocked him down, yet he got up and stood his ground more eagerly. Strength grows by being challenged. Each recovery makes the next one easier.
studyPrompts: When have you gotten back up after being knocked down?
What strengthened you?
What challenge in front of you might build strength?

entries.passageText: As to yourself, although you should live in such a way that you trust your own self with nothing which you could not entrust even to your enemy, yet, since certain matters occur which convention keeps secret, you should share with a friend at least all your worries and reflections. Regard him as loyal, and you will make him loyal. Some, for example, fearing to be deceived, have taught men to deceive; by their suspicions they have given their friend the right to do wrong. Why need I keep back any words in the presence of my friend? Why should I not regard myself as alone when in his company?
entries.reflection: Seneca says to share all your worries and reflections with a friend, and to regard him as loyal so that he becomes loyal. Trust is part of how friendship grows. Suspicion can make it fail.
studyPrompts: Whom do you share your worries with?
Whom could you trust more?
How do you show a friend you trust them?

entries.passageText: Let us, then, look carefully into the matter. It is likely that some troubles will befall us; but it is not a present fact. How often has the unexpected happened! How often has the expected never come to pass! And even though it is ordained to be, what does it avail to run out to meet your suffering? You will suffer soon enough, when it arrives; so look forward meanwhile to better things.
entries.reflection: Seneca notes how often the expected never happens and the unexpected does. You will suffer soon enough if trouble arrives; meanwhile, look forward to better things. Waiting does not have to mean dreading.
studyPrompts: What outcome are you waiting on?
Are you suffering it in advance?
What better thing could you look forward to?

entries.passageText: Speak both in the senate and to every man, whoever he may be, appropriately, not with any affectation: use plain discourse.
entries.reflection: Marcus advises speaking to everyone appropriately, without affectation, in plain language. Plain words are honest and respectful. They do not try to impress.
studyPrompts: Do you speak plainly?
When do you use words to impress rather than inform?
Whom could you speak to more simply and kindly?

entries.passageText: No man is tired of receiving what is useful. But it is useful to act according to nature. Do not then be tired of receiving what is useful by doing it to others.
entries.reflection: No one tires of receiving what is useful, says Marcus, and acting according to nature is useful, so do not tire of doing it for others. Helping others can renew you. Weariness can be eased by purpose.
studyPrompts: Where are you weary?
How might helping others refresh you?
What useful thing could you do today?

entries.passageText: How can our principles become dead, unless the impressions [thoughts] which correspond to them are extinguished? But it is in thy power continuously to fan these thoughts into a flame. I can have that opinion about anything which I ought to have. If I can, why am I disturbed? The things which are external to my mind have no relation at all to my mind.--Let this be the state of thy affects, and thou standest erect. To recover thy life is in thy power. Look at things again as thou didst use to look at them; for in this consists the recovery of thy life.
entries.reflection: Marcus says it is in your power to recover your life: look at things again as you once did. Principles can be rekindled. A new start is always available.
studyPrompts: What principle have you let fade?
How could you see things fresh?
What would recovering your life look like?

entries.passageText: From my mother, piety and beneficence, and abstinence, not only from evil deeds, but even from evil thoughts; and further, simplicity in my way of living, far removed from the habits of the rich.
entries.reflection: Marcus thanks his mother for teaching him simplicity in living, far from the habits of the rich. Simplicity is learned at home and kept by choice.
studyPrompts: What did your family teach you about simplicity?
What extra could you let go of?
What simple pleasure do you value?

entries.passageText: Why do you wait? Wisdom comes haphazard to no man. Money will come of its own accord; titles will be given to you; influence and authority will perhaps be thrust upon you; but virtue will not fall upon you by chance. Neither is knowledge thereof to be won by light effort or small toil; but toiling is worth while when one is about to win all goods at a single stroke.
entries.reflection: Seneca says money or titles may come by chance, but virtue never will. It takes real effort and is worth the toil. Some things can only be earned.
studyPrompts: What are you waiting to fall into your lap?
What is worth real effort?
What could you work at today?

entries.passageText: Men exist for the sake of one another. Teach them then, or bear with them.
entries.reflection: Marcus says people exist for the sake of one another: teach them, or bear with them. Respect means helping or tolerating, not despising. Both are choices.
studyPrompts: Whom do you find hard to bear?
Whom could you teach?
How could you show respect to someone who frustrates you?

entries.passageText: The Pythagoreans bid us in the morning look to the heavens that we may be reminded of those bodies which continually do the same things and in the same manner perform their work, and also be reminded of their purity and nudity. For there is no veil over a star.
entries.reflection: The Pythagoreans looked to the heavens in the morning to remember the steady order of the stars. Starting the day with a look at something larger steadies the mind.
studyPrompts: How do you start your day?
What reminds you of order and purpose?
What could you look at tomorrow morning?

entries.passageText: I shall therefore do as you bid, and shall gladly inform you by letter what I am doing, and in what sequence. I shall keep watching myself continually, and—a most useful habit—shall review each day. For this is what makes us wicked: that no one of us looks back over his own life. Our thoughts are devoted only to what we are about to do. And yet our plans for the future always depend on the past.
entries.reflection: Seneca resolves to review each day, because no one looks back over his own life. An evening review helps you learn from the day. The future depends on the past.
studyPrompts: What went well today?
What would you do differently?
What will you carry into tomorrow?

entries.passageText: But although virtues, when admitted, cannot depart and are easy to guard, yet the first steps in the approach to them are toilsome, because it is characteristic of a weak and diseased mind to fear that which is unfamiliar. The mind must, therefore, be forced to make a beginning; from then on, the medicine is not bitter; for just as soon as it is curing us it begins to give pleasure. One enjoys other cures only after health is restored, but a draught of philosophy is at the same moment wholesome and pleasant. Farewell.
entries.reflection: Seneca says the first steps toward a healthier mind are hard, but once the cure begins it becomes pleasant. Healing takes a start. The hardest part is beginning.
studyPrompts: What healing do you need?
What first step could you take?
Who could help you begin?

entries.passageText: He who does wrong does wrong against himself. He who acts unjustly acts unjustly to himself, because he makes himself bad.
entries.reflection: Marcus says that one who does wrong wrongs himself, because he makes himself bad. Guilt is a signal that we have harmed ourselves as well as others. It points back to who we want to be.
studyPrompts: What wrong are you carrying?
How has it affected you?
What could you do to set it right?

entries.passageText: I claim you for myself; you are my handiwork. When I saw your abilities, I laid my hand upon you, I exhorted you, I applied the goad and did not permit you to march lazily, but roused you continually. And now I do the same; but by this time I am cheering on one who is in the race and so in turn cheers me on.
entries.reflection: Seneca tells Lucilius he once urged him on, and now cheers him as he runs, while Lucilius cheers him in return. Encouragement goes both ways. Those we encourage can encourage us.
studyPrompts: Who cheered you on?
Whom do you cheer on now?
How could you encourage someone today?

entries.passageText: all that you behold, that which comprises both god and man, is one—we are the parts of one great body. Nature produced us related to one another, since she created us from the same source and to the same end. She engendered in us mutual affection, and made us prone to friendships. She established fairness and justice; according to her ruling, it is more wretched to commit than to suffer injury. Through her orders, let our hands be ready for all that needs to be helped.
entries.reflection: Seneca says we are parts of one great body, born related to each other and made for friendship and mutual help. Unity is natural. Let your hands be ready to help.
studyPrompts: Where do you feel part of something larger?
Whom could you help today?
What breaks unity around you?

entries.passageText: Everything has two handles, the one by which it may be borne, the other by which it may not. If your brother acts unjustly, do not lay hold of the act by that handle wherein he acts unjustly, for this is the handle which cannot be borne; but lay hold of the other, that he is your brother, that he was nurtured with you, and you will lay hold of the thing by that handle by which it can be borne.
entries.reflection: Epictetus says everything has two handles. If your brother wrongs you, take hold of the handle that he is your brother, not the one that he wronged you. Peace begins with which handle you choose.
studyPrompts: Whom are you in conflict with?
What other handle could you take?
How would that change the situation?

entries.passageText: Then comes the second problem,—how to deal with men. What is our purpose? What precepts do we offer? Should we bid them refrain from bloodshed? What a little thing it is not to harm one whom you ought to help! It is indeed worthy of great praise, when man treats man with kindness! Shall we advise stretching forth the hand to the shipwrecked sailor, or pointing out the way to the wanderer, or sharing a crust with the starving? Yes, if I can only tell you first everything which ought to be afforded or withheld; meantime, I can lay down for mankind a rule, in short compass, for our duties in human relationships:
entries.reflection: Seneca asks whether we should advise helping the shipwrecked, guiding the lost, and sharing bread with the hungry. Kindness to strangers is a basic human duty.
studyPrompts: Who is lost or hungry around you?
What could you share?
When has a stranger helped you?

entries.passageText: From my grandfather Verus [I learned] good morals and the government of my temper. From the reputation and remembrance of my father, modesty and a manly character.
entries.reflection: Marcus begins his Meditations by thanking his grandfather for good morals and his father for modesty. We carry our families' lessons. Gratitude for them is a good place to start.
studyPrompts: What did your family teach you?
Whom in your family are you grateful for?
What lesson would you like to pass on?

entries.passageText: If you ask how one can make oneself a friend quickly, I will tell you, provided we are agreed that I may pay my debt at once and square the account, so far as this letter is concerned. Hecato, says: “I can show you a philtre, compounded without drugs, herbs, or any witch’s incantation: ‘If you would be loved, love.’” Now there is great pleasure, not only in maintaining old and established friendships, but also in beginning and acquiring new ones.
entries.reflection: Seneca quotes Hecato: if you want to be loved, love. Love is not something to wait for. It begins with giving it.
studyPrompts: Whom do you love?
How do you show it?
Whom could you love better?

entries.passageText: Therefore continually remind yourself, Lucilius, how many ambitions you have attained. When you see many ahead of you, think how many are behind! If you would thank the gods, and be grateful for your past life, you should contemplate how many men you have outstripped. But what have you to do with the others? You have outstripped yourself.
entries.reflection: Seneca advises: when you see many ahead of you, think how many are behind. Comparison breeds envy. Better to see how far you have come.
studyPrompts: Whom do you compare yourself to?
How far have you come?
What are you grateful for in your progress?

entries.passageText: Beasts avoid the dangers which they see, and when they have escaped them are free from care; but we men torment ourselves over that which is to come as well as over that which is past. Many of our blessings bring bane to us; for memory recalls the tortures of fear, while foresight anticipates them. The present alone can make no man wretched. Farewell.
entries.reflection: Seneca observes that animals avoid the danger in front of them and then are free from care, but we torment ourselves over both future and past. The present alone does not make us wretched.
studyPrompts: What are you worrying about in the future?
What from the past still torments you?
What is good in this present moment?

entries.passageText: Everything which happens either happens in such wise as thou art formed by nature to bear it, or as thou art not formed by nature to bear it. If, then, it happens to thee in such way as thou art formed by nature to bear it, do not complain, but bear it as thou art formed by nature to bear it. But if it happens in such wise as thou art not formed by nature to bear it, do not complain, for it will perish after it has consumed thee. Remember, however, that thou art formed by nature to bear everything, with respect to which it depends on thy own opinion to make it endurable and tolerable, by thinking that it is either thy interest or thy duty to do this.
entries.reflection: Marcus says not to complain about what happens, and that you are formed to bear anything your own judgment can make tolerable, by seeing it as your interest or your duty. Opinion makes much of the difference.
studyPrompts: What hardship are you facing?
How might you see it differently?
What helps you bear things?

entries.passageText: We ought to see to it that we flee to the greatest possible distance from provocations to vice. We should toughen our minds, and remove them far from the allurements of pleasure. A single winter relaxed Hannibal’s fibre; his pampering in Campania took the vigour out of that hero who had triumphed over Alpine snows. He conquered with his weapons, but was conquered by his vices.
entries.reflection: Seneca says one soft winter undid Hannibal, who conquered with weapons but was conquered by vice. Discipline can be lost in comfort. Guard against allurements.
studyPrompts: What comfort or pleasure might weaken you?
What helps you stay disciplined?
Where do you need to toughen your mind?

entries.passageText: “Then how can I free myself?” you ask. You cannot escape necessities, but you can overcome them. By force a way is made. And this way will be afforded you by philosophy. Betake yourself therefore to philosophy if you would be safe, untroubled, happy, in fine, if you wish to be,—and that is most important,—free. There is no other way to attain this end.
entries.reflection: Seneca says you cannot escape necessities, but you can overcome them, and philosophy is the way to be free. Freedom is an inner state. It can be practiced anywhere.
studyPrompts: What necessity constrains you?
How could you overcome it inwardly?
What does inner freedom mean to you?

entries.passageText: A good conscience welcomes the crowd, but a bad conscience, even in solitude, is disturbed and troubled. If your deeds are honourable, let everybody know them; if base, what matters it that no one knows them, as long as you yourself know them? How wretched you are if you despise such a witness! Farewell.
entries.reflection: Seneca says a good conscience welcomes witnesses, while a bad one is troubled even in solitude. If your deeds are honorable, let everyone know; if not, you still know.
studyPrompts: Would your actions welcome witnesses?
What does your conscience tell you?
What honorable thing could you do today?

entries.passageText: Let this be the kernel of my idea: let us say what we feel, and feel what we say; let speech harmonize with life. That man has fulfilled his promise who is the same person both when you see him and when you hear him.
entries.reflection: Seneca says we should say what we feel and feel what we say, letting speech match life. A person keeps their promise when they are the same whether seen or heard.
studyPrompts: Does your speech match your life?
What promise do you need to keep?
Where is there a gap between what you say and do?

entries.passageText: It is satisfaction to a man to do the proper works of a man. Now it is a proper work of a man to be benevolent to his own kind, to despise the movements of the senses, to form a just judgment of plausible appearances, and to take a survey of the nature of the universe and of the things which happen in it.
entries.reflection: Marcus says it is satisfying to do the proper work of a human being, which includes being kind to others. Good deeds are natural and fulfilling.
studyPrompts: What is the proper work of a human being for you?
What kindness could you do today?
What satisfies you most?

entries.passageText: Take pleasure in one thing and rest in it, in passing from one social act to another social act, thinking of God.
entries.reflection: Marcus finds rest in passing from one act for others to the next. A life of service can be a source of peace, not just effort.
studyPrompts: What act for others could you do today?
Where do you find rest?
How could service bring you peace?

entries.passageText: That which is short of perfection must necessarily be unsteady, at one time progressing, at another slipping or growing faint; and it will surely slip back unless it keeps struggling ahead; for if a man slackens at all in zeal and faithful application, he must retrograde. No one can resume his progress at the point where he left off.
entries.reflection: Seneca warns that anyone who slackens in faithful effort slips back. Faithfulness is steady effort over time. Progress needs to be kept up.
studyPrompts: Where have you slackened?
What would faithful effort look like?
What progress do you want to keep?

entries.passageText: Whatever any one does or says, I must be good; just as if the gold, or the emerald, or the purple, were always saying this. Whatever any one does or says, I must be emerald and keep my color.
entries.reflection: Marcus says whatever anyone does or says, he must be good, like an emerald that keeps its color. Character does not depend on others' behavior.
studyPrompts: Whose behavior tempts you to change your own?
What is your color?
How could you keep it today?

entries.passageText: Nothing, Lucilius, is ours, except time. We were entrusted by nature with the ownership of this single thing, so fleeting and slippery that anyone who will can oust us from possession. What fools these mortals be! They allow the cheapest and most useless things, which can easily be replaced, to be charged in the reckoning, after they have acquired them; but they never regard themselves as in debt when they have received some of that precious commodity,—time! And yet time is the one loan which even a grateful recipient cannot repay.
entries.reflection: Seneca says nothing is ours except time, yet we let it slip and never count its cost. Time is the one loan we cannot repay. Use it well.
studyPrompts: Where does your time go?
What would you do with more time?
How could you spend today's time well?

entries.passageText: You should keep learning as long as you are ignorant,—even to the end of your life, if there is anything in the proverb. And the proverb suits the present case as well as any: “As long as you live, keep learning how to live.” For all that, there is also something which I can teach in that school. You ask, do you, what I can teach? That even an old man should keep learning.
entries.reflection: Seneca says to keep learning as long as you are ignorant, even to the end of life: as long as you live, keep learning how to live. Learning has no finish line.
studyPrompts: What are you learning now?
What do you want to learn?
Who could teach you?

entries.passageText: Everything harmonizes with me, which is harmonious to thee, O Universe. Nothing for me is too early nor too late, which is in due time for thee. Everything is fruit to me which thy seasons bring, O Nature: from thee are all things, in thee are all things, to thee all things return. The poet says, Dear city of Cecrops; and wilt not thou say, Dear city of Zeus?
entries.reflection: Marcus says everything that fits the universe fits him; all things come from nature and return to it. The Stoics saw themselves as part of a larger whole.
studyPrompts: Where do you feel part of nature?
What does belonging to a larger whole mean to you?
Where could you notice nature today?

entries.passageText: Does the light of the lamp shine without losing its splendor until it is extinguished? and shall the truth which is in thee and justice and temperance be extinguished [before thy death]?
entries.reflection: Marcus asks whether a lamp's light shines until it goes out, and whether your truth, justice and self-control should go out before you do. Keep your light burning.
studyPrompts: What light do you carry?
What threatens to dim it?
How could you keep it burning?

entries.passageText: Socrates made the same remark to one who complained; he said: “Why do you wonder that globe-trotting does not help you, seeing that you always take yourself with you? The reason which set you wandering is ever at your heels.” What pleasure is there in seeing new lands? Or in surveying cities and spots of interest? All your bustle is useless. Do you ask why such flight does not help you? It is because you flee along with yourself. You must lay aside the burdens of the mind; until you do this, no place will satisfy you.
entries.reflection: Seneca quotes Socrates: travel does not help because you take yourself with you. Lay aside the burdens of the mind first. Then any place can satisfy you.
studyPrompts: What burden of the mind are you carrying?
What would laying it aside look like?
Who could help you with it?

entries.passageText: This is a fine saying of Plato: That he who is discoursing about men should look also at earthly things as if he viewed them from some higher place; should look at them in their assemblies, armies, agricultural labors, marriages, treaties, births, deaths, noise of the courts of justice, desert places, various nations of barbarians, feasts, lamentations, markets, a mixture of all things and an orderly combination of contraries.
entries.reflection: Marcus repeats Plato's advice to look at human affairs as if from above: the assemblies, farms, marriages, births and deaths together. Seen from a height, our worries take their place in a larger picture.
studyPrompts: What would your current problem look like from above?
What else is part of the picture?
How does that change your view?

entries.passageText: “But,” you reply, “I wish to dip first into one book and then into another.” I tell you that it is the sign of an overnice appetite to toy with many dishes; for when they are manifold and varied, they cloy but do not nourish. So you should always read standard authors; and when you crave a change, fall back upon those whom you read before. Each day acquire something that will fortify you against poverty, against death, indeed against other misfortunes as well; and after you have run over many thoughts, select one to be thoroughly digested that day.
entries.reflection: Seneca advises acquiring one useful thought each day and digesting it well. Small daily gains add up. You do not need to learn everything at once.
studyPrompts: What one thought could you take from today?
What small daily habit could you build?
What have small steps achieved for you?

entries.passageText: That trouble once removed, all change of scene will become pleasant; though you may be driven to the uttermost ends of the earth, in whatever corner of a savage land you may find yourself, that place, however forbidding, will be to you a hospitable abode. The person you are matters more than the place to which you go; for that reason we should not make the mind a bondsman to any one place. Live in this belief: “I am not born for any one corner of the universe; this whole world is my country.”
entries.reflection: Seneca says: I am not born for any one corner of the universe; this whole world is my country. The person you are matters more than the place you go.
studyPrompts: Where do you feel you belong?
How do you carry belonging with you?
How could you help someone feel at home?

entries.passageText: The young character, which cannot hold fast to righteousness, must be rescued from the mob; it is too easy to side with the majority. Even Socrates, Cato, and Laelius might have been shaken in their moral strength by a crowd that was unlike them; so true it is that none of us, no matter how much he cultivates his abilities, can withstand the shock of faults that approach, as it were, with so great a retinue.
entries.reflection: Seneca warns that even Socrates, Cato and Laelius could have been shaken by a crowd unlike them. It is easy to side with the majority. Moral courage means holding to what is right anyway.
studyPrompts: When have you felt pressure to go along with the crowd?
What helps you hold firm?
Who supports your values?

entries.passageText: But the fact is, the same thing is advantageous to me which is advantageous to you; for I am not your friend unless whatever is at issue concerning you is my concern also. Friendship produces between us a partnership in all our interests. There is no such thing as good or bad fortune for the individual; we live in common. And no one can live happily who has regard to himself alone and transforms everything into a question of his own utility; you must live for your neighbour, if you would live for yourself.
entries.reflection: Seneca says no one lives happily who considers only himself: you must live for your neighbor if you would live for yourself. Our lives are bound together.
studyPrompts: Who are your neighbors?
How do you live for them?
What could you do for them this week?

entries.passageText: But whatever you do, come back soon from body to mind. The mind must be exercised both day and night, for it is nourished by moderate labour; and this form of exercise need not be hampered by cold or hot weather, or even by old age. Cultivate that good which improves with the years.
entries.reflection: Seneca says to return quickly from body to mind; the mind must be exercised day and night. Physical training matters, but so does mental training.
studyPrompts: How do you exercise your mind?
How is your mental health?
What could you do for your mind today?

entries.passageText: He says: “Contented poverty is an honourable estate.” Indeed, if it be contented, it is not poverty at all. It is not the man who has too little, but the man who craves more, that is poor. What does it matter how much a man has laid up in his safe, or in his warehouse, how large are his flocks and how fat his dividends, if he covets his neighbour’s property, and reckons, not his past gains, but his hopes of gains to come? Do you ask what is the proper limit to wealth? It is, first, to have what is necessary, and, second, to have what is enough. Farewell.
entries.reflection: Seneca says it is not the person who has too little, but the one who craves more, who is poor. The proper limit to wealth is what is necessary, then what is enough.
studyPrompts: What is enough for you?
What do you crave?
How could you be content with less?

entries.passageText: For my part, I do not agree with him. To me, the thought of my dead friends is sweet and appealing. For I have had them as if I should one day lose them; I have lost them as if I have them still. Therefore, Lucilius, act as befits your own serenity of mind, and cease to put a wrong interpretation on the gifts of Fortune. Fortune has taken away, but Fortune has given.
entries.reflection: Seneca says the thought of his dead friends is sweet: he had them as one who would lose them, and lost them as one who has them still. Remembering can bring warmth as well as pain.
studyPrompts: Whom do you remember?
What sweet memories do you have of them?
How do you still have them?

entries.passageText: But both courses are to be avoided; you should not copy the bad simply because they are many, nor should you hate the many because they are unlike you. Withdraw into yourself, as far as you can. Associate with those who will make a better man of you. Welcome those whom you yourself can improve. The process is mutual; for men learn while they teach.
entries.reflection: Seneca says to keep company with people who will improve you, and welcome those you can improve, because people learn while they teach. Mentoring benefits both sides.
studyPrompts: Who improves you?
Whom could you improve?
What have you learned while teaching?

entries.passageText: Keep on as you have begun, and make all possible haste, so that you may have longer enjoyment of an improved mind, one that is at peace with itself. Doubtless you will derive enjoyment during the time when you are improving your mind and setting it at peace with itself; but quite different is the pleasure which comes from contemplation when one’s mind is so cleansed from every stain that it shines.
entries.reflection: Seneca urges Lucilius to keep on as he has begun and to hurry, so he may enjoy a mind at peace with itself. The road ahead is about continuing what you have started.
studyPrompts: What have you begun?
What would it mean to keep going?
What kind of mind do you want to have at the end of the road?

entries.passageText: If you desire philosophy, prepare yourself from the beginning to be ridiculed, to expect that many will sneer at you, and say, He has all at once returned to us as a philosopher; and whence does he get this supercilious look for us? Do you not show a supercilious look; but hold on to the things which seem to you best as one appointed by God to this station. And remember that if you abide in the same principles, these men who first ridiculed will afterwards admire you; but if you shall have been overpowered by them, you will bring on yourself double ridicule.
entries.reflection: Epictetus warns that anyone who begins to live by principle will be mocked at first; hold on, and those who laughed may come to admire you. Beginnings take courage.
studyPrompts: What are you beginning?
What ridicule do you fear?
What will help you hold on?

entries.passageText: When you are going to take in hand any act remind yourself what kind of an act it is. If you are going to bathe, place before yourself what happens in the bath; some splashing the water, others pushing against one another, others abusing one another, and some stealing; and thus with more safety you will undertake the matter, if you say to yourself, I now intend to bathe, and to maintain my will in a manner conformable to nature. And so you will do in every act; for thus if any hindrance to bathing shall happen let this thought be ready. It was not this only that I intended, but I intended also to maintain my will in a way conformable to nature; but I shall not maintain it so if I am vexed at what happens.
entries.reflection: Epictetus advises picturing what an activity involves before you start, so that setbacks do not throw you. Preparing the mind is part of preparing for the task.
studyPrompts: What are you about to do?
What might go wrong?
How will you keep your composure?

entries.passageText: Is my understanding sufficient for this or not? If it is sufficient, I use it for the work as an instrument given by the universal nature. But if it is not sufficient, then either I retire from the work and give way to him who is able to do it better, unless there be some reason why I ought not to do so; or I do it as well as I can, taking to help me the man who with the aid of my ruling principle can do what is now fit and useful for the general good. For what-soever either by myself or with another I can do, ought to be directed to this only, to that which is useful and well suited to society.
entries.reflection: Marcus asks whether he is up to a task. If not, he gives way to someone better, or takes on a helper. Good teamwork means knowing when to lead and when to ask for help.
studyPrompts: Is your understanding sufficient for your current task?
Who could help you?
When should you give way to someone better?

entries.passageText: Either it is a well-arranged universe or a chaos huddled together, but still a universe. But can a certain order subsist in thee, and disorder in the All? And this too when all things are so separated and diffused and sympathetic.
entries.reflection: Marcus admits he does not know whether the universe is ordered or chaos, yet he asks whether there can be order in him. Even in doubt, you can keep order within.
studyPrompts: What are you unsure about?
What order can you keep within?
How do you live with doubt?

entries.passageText: If ever you have come upon a grove that is full of ancient trees which have grown to an unusual height, shutting out a view of the sky by a veil of pleached and intertwining branches, then the loftiness of the forest, the seclusion of the spot, and your marvel at the thick unbroken shade in the midst of the open spaces, will prove to you the presence of deity. Or if a cave, made by the deep crumbling of the rocks, holds up a mountain on its arch, a place not built with hands but hollowed out into such spaciousness by natural causes, your soul will be deeply moved by a certain intimation of the existence of God. We worship the sources of mighty rivers; we erect altars at places where great streams burst suddenly from hidden sources; we adore springs of hot water as divine, and consecrate certain pools because of their dark waters or their immeasurable depth.
entries.reflection: Seneca describes a grove of ancient trees, a cave in the rock, or a spring bursting from the ground, and the awe they stir. Nature can move the soul.
studyPrompts: What place has filled you with awe?
When did you last feel wonder?
Where could you find it today?

entries.passageText: In walking about, as you take care not to step on a nail, or to sprain your foot, so take care not to damage your own ruling faculty; and if we observe this rule in every act, we shall undertake this act with more security.
entries.reflection: Epictetus says to guard your ruling faculty as carefully as you avoid stepping on a nail. Vigilance applies to the mind too.
studyPrompts: What damages your judgment?
How do you guard your mind?
What would more care look like?

entries.passageText: This is also a source of no mean joy and profit; for what is sweeter than to be so valued by one’s wife that one becomes more valuable to oneself for this reason? Hence my dear Paulina is able to make me responsible, not only for her fears, but also for my own.
entries.reflection: Seneca says it is sweet to be so valued by his wife Paulina that he becomes more valuable to himself, and takes care of himself for her sake. Love can make us care for ourselves.
studyPrompts: Who values you?
How do you care for yourself for their sake?
How could you show your partner they are valued?

entries.passageText: Practise thyself even in the things which thou despairest of accomplishing. For even the left hand, which is ineffectual for all other things for want of practice, holds the bridle more vigorously than the right hand; for it has been practised in this.
entries.reflection: Marcus says to practise even the things you despair of, as the left hand grows strong at holding reins through practice. Failure is part of training.
studyPrompts: Where have you failed?
What could you practise?
What has practice taught you before?

entries.passageText: The yield of poor mines is on the surface; those are really rich whose veins lurk deep, and they will make more bountiful returns to him who delves unceasingly. So too those baubles which delight the common crowd afford but a thin pleasure, laid on as a coating, and every joy that is only plated lacks a real basis. But the joy of which I speak, that to which I am endeavouring to lead you, is something solid, disclosing itself the more fully as you penetrate into it.
entries.reflection: Seneca says shallow pleasures are only plated, while real joy runs deep like a rich vein of ore. Good laughter grows out of something solid.
studyPrompts: What brings you real joy?
What pleasures are only surface?
Who makes you laugh in a way that lasts?

entries.passageText: First, do nothing inconsiderately, nor without a purpose. Second, make thy acts refer to nothing else than to a social end.
entries.reflection: Marcus gives two rules: do nothing inconsiderately or without purpose, and direct your acts to the common good. Prudence in a sentence.
studyPrompts: What are you about to do without thinking?
What is your purpose?
How does it serve others?

entries.passageText: And we ought to bear the absence of friends cheerfully, just because everyone is bound to be often absent from his friends even when they are present. Include among such cases, in the first place, the nights spent apart, then the different engagements which each of two friends has, then the private studies of each and their excursions into the country, and you will see that foreign travel does not rob us of much.
entries.reflection: Seneca says we should bear the absence of friends cheerfully, since even when together we are often apart. Distance does not take away as much as it seems.
studyPrompts: Whom do you miss?
How do you stay close at a distance?
What helps you bear absence?

entries.passageText: Neither in writing nor in reading wilt thou be able to lay down rules for others before thou shalt have first learned to obey rules thyself. Much more is this so in life.
entries.reflection: Marcus says you cannot lay down rules for others until you have learned to obey rules yourself. Obedience prepares us to lead.
studyPrompts: What rules do you find hard to follow?
How has following taught you to lead?
What rule could you keep better?

entries.passageText: If we had the privilege of looking into a good man’s soul, oh what a fair, holy, magnificent, gracious, and shining face should we behold—radiant on the one side with justice and temperance, on another with bravery and wisdom! And, besides these, thriftiness, moderation, endurance, refinement, affability, and—though hard to believe—love of one’s fellow-men, that Good which is so rare in man, all these would be shedding their own glory over that soul. There, too, forethought combined with elegance and, resulting from these, a most excellent greatness of soul (the noblest of all these virtues)—indeed what charm, O ye heavens, what authority and dignity would they contribute! What a wonderful combination of sweetness and power! No one could call such a face lovable without also calling it worshipful.
entries.reflection: Seneca imagines seeing a good person's soul, radiant with justice, courage, wisdom and love of others. The most beautiful thing is good character.
studyPrompts: Whose character do you find beautiful?
What virtues would you like to shine in you?
How could you notice beauty in others?

entries.passageText: If any person was intending to put your body in the power of any man whom you fell in with on the way, you would be vexed; but that you put your understanding in the power of any man whom you meet, so that if he should revile you, it is disturbed and troubled, are you not ashamed at this?
entries.reflection: Epictetus asks why we would let anyone who insults us disturb our mind, when we would never hand them our body. Shame belongs to how we respond, not to what others say.
studyPrompts: Whose words disturb you?
Who controls your mind?
What would it look like to keep your own judgment?

entries.passageText: If thou hadst a step-mother and a mother at the same time, thou wouldst be dutiful to thy step-mother, but still thou wouldst constantly return to thy mother. Let the court and philosophy now be to thee step-mother and mother: return to philosophy frequently and repose in her, through whom what thou meetest with in the court appears to thee tolerable, and thou appearest tolerable in the court.
entries.reflection: Marcus compares the court to a step-mother you are dutiful to, and philosophy to a mother you return to. The image recalls the bond of returning to the one who raised you.
studyPrompts: Who raised you?
What do you return to them for?
How could you honor them?

entries.passageText: Be not elated at any advantage (excellence) which belongs to another. If a horse when he is elated should say, I am beautiful, one might endure it. But when you are elated, and say, I have a beautiful horse, you must know that you are elated at having a good horse. What then is your own? The use of appearances. Consequently when in the use of appearances you are conformable to nature, then be elated, for then you will be elated at something good which is your own.
entries.reflection: Epictetus says not to be proud of a fine horse as if its excellence were yours. Real success is in how you use your own mind.
studyPrompts: What successes are truly yours?
What do you take pride in that is not yours?
How would you measure success differently?

entries.passageText: But my letter calls for its closing sentence. Hear and take to heart this useful and wholesome motto: “Cherish some man of high character, and keep him ever before your eyes, living as if he were watching you, and ordering all your actions as if he beheld them.”
entries.reflection: Seneca quotes Epicurus: keep someone of good character before your eyes, and live as if they were watching. On a long watch, imagine who you would want to see you.
studyPrompts: Whose example do you carry with you?
How would you act if they were watching?
What does your watch reveal about your character?

entries.passageText: You have been complaining that my letters to you are rather carelessly written. Now who talks carefully unless he also desires to talk affectedly? I prefer that my letters should be just what my conversation would be if you and I were sitting in one another’s company or taking walks together,—spontaneous and easy; for my letters have nothing strained or artificial about them.
entries.reflection: Seneca says he wants his letters to sound like his conversation, spontaneous and easy, with nothing strained or artificial. Sincerity is being the same in word and in person.
studyPrompts: Do you speak differently in writing than in person?
Where are you being artificial?
How could you be more genuine?

entries.passageText: The best way of avenging thyself is not to become like [the wrong-doer].
entries.reflection: Marcus says the best revenge is not to become like the one who wronged you. That keeps your character your own.
studyPrompts: Who has wronged you?
Are you becoming like them?
What would the best revenge look like?

entries.passageText: To-day I have got out of all trouble, or rather I have cast out all trouble, for it was not outside, but within and in my opinions.
entries.reflection: Marcus says he got rid of his troubles today, because they were not outside but in his opinions. Stress often lives in how we see things.
studyPrompts: What is stressing you?
Which part is your opinion about it?
What would seeing it differently change?

entries.passageText: My baker is out of bread; but the overseer, or the house-steward, or one of my tenants can supply me therewith. “Bad bread!” you say. But just wait for it; it will become good. Hunger will make even such bread delicate and of the finest flavour. For that reason I must not eat until hunger bids me; so I shall wait and shall not eat until I can either get good bread or else cease to be squeamish about it.
entries.reflection: Seneca jokes that bad bread becomes good if you wait until you are hungry. Hunger is the best sauce, and gratitude comes easier with need.
studyPrompts: What simple food are you thankful for?
How has hardship changed your tastes?
What everyday thing do you take for granted?

entries.passageText: From Catulus not to be indifferent when a friend finds fault, even if he should find fault without reason, but to try to restore him to his usual disposition; and to be ready to speak well of teachers, as it is reported of Domitius and Athenodotus; and to love my children truly.
entries.reflection: Among the lessons he learned from his teacher Catulus, Marcus lists to love his children truly. Loving children well is something we learn.
studyPrompts: What children are in your life?
What does loving them truly look like?
What did you learn from those who loved you?

entries.passageText: These reasonings do not cohere: I am richer than you, therefore I am better than you; I am more eloquent than you, therefore I am better than you. On the contrary, these rather cohere: I am richer than you, therefore my possessions are greater than yours; I am more eloquent than you, therefore my speech is superior to yours. But you are neither possession nor speech.
entries.reflection: Epictetus says being richer or more eloquent does not make you better; you are neither your property nor your speech. Pride confuses what we have with who we are.
studyPrompts: What are you proud of?
Is it who you are or what you have?
What would humility look like?

entries.passageText: From Alexander the grammarian, to refrain from fault-finding, and not in a reproachful way to chide those who uttered any barbarous or solecistic or strange-sounding expression; but dexterously to introduce the very expression which ought to have been used, and in the way of answer or giving confirmation, or joining in an inquiry about the thing itself, not about the word, or by some other fit suggestion.
