entries.reflection: Marcus learned from Alexander not to correct people's mistakes harshly, but to model the right word kindly. Courtesy corrects without shaming.
studyPrompts: How do you correct others?
When have you been corrected kindly?
How could you be more courteous today?

entries.passageText: Dost thou wish to be praised by a man who curses himself thrice every hour? wouldst thou wish to please a man who does not please himself? Does a man please himself who repents of nearly everything that he does?
entries.reflection: Marcus asks whether you would want praise from someone who curses himself constantly and repents of nearly everything. Endless self-reproach does not help. Learn and move on.
studyPrompts: What do you keep regretting?
What have you learned from it?
What would moving on look like?

entries.passageText: What then? Shall I not follow in the footsteps of my predecessors? I shall indeed use the old road, but if I find one that makes a shorter cut and is smoother to travel, I shall open the new road. Men who have made these discoveries before us are not our masters, but our guides. Truth lies open for all; it has not yet been monopolized. And there is plenty of it left even for posterity to discover. Farewell.
entries.reflection: Seneca says he will use the old road, but open a new one if it is shorter and smoother. Those who went before are guides, not masters.
studyPrompts: What road are you on?
Who are your guides?
Where might you need a new road?

entries.passageText: From my governor, to be neither of the green nor of the blue party at the games in the Circus, nor a partisan either of the Parmularius or the Scutarius at the gladiators' fights; from him too I learned endurance of labor, and to want little, and to work with my own hands, and not to meddle with other people's affairs, and not to be ready to listen to slander.
entries.reflection: Marcus learned from his tutor not to take sides at the games, to work with his own hands, and not to listen to slander. Fairness starts with refusing to be partisan.
studyPrompts: Where do you take sides too quickly?
Do you listen to slander?
What would fairness look like today?

entries.passageText: If a thing is difficult to be accomplished by thyself, do not think that it is impossible for man: but if anything is possible for man and conformable to his nature, think that this can be attained by thyself too.
entries.reflection: Marcus says that if something is hard for you, do not think it impossible; if it is possible for people, it is possible for you. Discouragement shrinks what you can do.
studyPrompts: What feels impossible right now?
Who has done it before?
What first step could you take?

entries.passageText: Begin the morning by saying to thyself, I shall meet with the busybody, the ungrateful, arrogant, deceitful, envious, unsocial. All these things happen to them by reason of their ignorance of what is good and evil. But I who have seen the nature of the good that it is beautiful, and of the bad that it is ugly, and the nature of him who does wrong, that it is akin to me; not [only] of the same blood or seed, but that it participates in [the same] intelligence and [the same] portion of the divinity, I can neither be injured by any of them, for no one can fix on me what is ugly, nor can I be angry with my kinsman, nor hate him. For we are made for co-operation, like feet, like hands, like eyelids, like the rows of the upper and lower teeth. To act against one another, then, is contrary to nature; and it is acting against one another to be vexed and to turn away.
entries.reflection: Marcus reminds himself each morning that even difficult people are his kin, sharing the same reason, and that we are made to work together like hands and feet. Kinship goes beyond blood.
studyPrompts: Who are your brothers and sisters?
Whom do you find hard to see as kin?
How could you work together better?

entries.passageText: Let no act be done without a purpose, nor otherwise than according to the perfect principles of art.
entries.reflection: Marcus says to do nothing without purpose, and nothing short of the best principles of your craft. Excellence is purpose plus skill.
studyPrompts: What is your craft?
What would excellent work look like today?
What purpose drives you?

entries.passageText: ’Twas night, and all the world was lulled to rest. This is not true; for no real rest can be found when reason has not done the lulling. Night brings our troubles to the light, rather than banishes them; it merely changes the form of our worries. For even when we seek slumber, our sleepless moments are as harassing as the daytime. Real tranquillity is the state reached by an unperverted mind when it is relaxed.
entries.reflection: Seneca says night brings troubles to light rather than banishing them; real rest comes when reason has calmed the mind. If sleeplessness persists, speak to a medic or chaplain.
studyPrompts: What troubles come to light at night?
What calms your mind?
Who could help if you have not been sleeping?

entries.passageText: The Lacedaemonians at their public spectacles used to set seats in the shade for strangers, but themselves sat down anywhere.
entries.reflection: Marcus notes that the Spartans gave strangers seats in the shade, and sat anywhere themselves. Hospitality puts the guest first.
studyPrompts: Who is a stranger around you?
How could you give them the better seat?
When were you welcomed this way?

entries.passageText: How easy it is to repel and to wipe away every impression which is troublesome or unsuitable, and immediately to be in all tranquillity.
entries.reflection: Marcus says how easy it is to push away a troubling impression and be at once in tranquillity. Calm can be a choice made quickly.
studyPrompts: What impression is troubling you?
Could you set it aside?
What helps you return to calm?

entries.passageText: Does a man bathe quickly (early)? do not say that he bathes badly, but that he bathes quickly. Does a man drink much wine? do not say that he does this badly, but say that he drinks much. For before you shall have determined the opinion how do you know whether he is acting wrong? Thus it will not happen to you to comprehend some appearances which are capable of being comprehended, but to assent to others.
entries.reflection: Epictetus says do not say someone bathes badly, only that he bathes quickly; you do not know his reasons. Gossip often judges before it knows.
studyPrompts: What have you judged without knowing?
How could you describe instead of judging?
Whose reputation could you protect?

entries.passageText: I disagree with those who strike out into the midst of the billows and, welcoming a stormy existence, wrestle daily in hardihood of soul with life’s problems. The wise man will endure all that, but will not choose it; he will prefer to be at peace rather than at war. It helps little to have cast out your own faults if you must quarrel with those of others.
entries.reflection: Seneca says the wise will endure storms, but will not seek them out; they prefer peace to war. Endurance does not mean looking for trouble.
studyPrompts: What storm are you enduring?
Are you seeking out trouble?
What would choosing peace look like?

entries.passageText: A man should always have these two rules in readiness; the one to do only whatever the reason of the ruling and legislating faculty may suggest for the use of men; the other, to change thy opinion, if there is any one at hand who sets thee right and moves thee from any opinion. But this change of opinion must proceed only from a certain persuasion, as of what is just or of common advantage, and the like, not because it appears pleasant or brings reputation.
entries.reflection: Marcus says to be ready to change your opinion if someone sets you right, as long as you are persuaded by reason. Good advice deserves a hearing.
studyPrompts: What advice have you resisted?
Whose counsel do you trust?
What would it take to change your mind?

entries.passageText: It is time to stop, but not before I have paid duty. “The knowledge of sin is the beginning of salvation.” This saying of Epicurus seems to me to be a noble one. For he who does not know that he has sinned does not desire correction; you must discover yourself in the wrong before you can reform yourself.
entries.reflection: Seneca quotes Epicurus: knowledge of sin is the beginning of salvation. You must find yourself in the wrong before you can put it right.
studyPrompts: Where are you in the wrong?
Whom do you owe an apology?
What would putting it right look like?

entries.passageText: Both man and God and the universe produce fruit; at the proper seasons each produces it. But and if usage has especially fixed these terms to the vine and like things, this is nothing. Reason produces fruit both for all and for itself, and there are produced from it other things of the same kind as reason itself.
entries.reflection: Marcus says people, the universe and reason all bear fruit in their proper seasons. Each season has its harvest.
studyPrompts: What season are you in?
What fruit is it bearing?
What are you waiting to ripen?

entries.passageText: I am so firmly determined, however, to test the constancy of your mind that, drawing from the teachings of great men, I shall give you also a lesson: Set aside a certain number of days, during which you shall be content with the scantiest and cheapest fare, with coarse and rough dress, saying to yourself the while: “Is this the condition that I feared?”
entries.reflection: Seneca suggests setting aside a few days to live on the cheapest food and roughest clothes, and asking, is this what I feared? Practising hardship takes away its fear.
studyPrompts: What do you fear losing?
What could you go without for a few days?
What might you learn?

entries.passageText: When any person treats you ill or speaks ill of you, remember that he does this or says this because he thinks that it is his duty. It is not possible then for him to follow that which seems right to you, but that which seems right to himself. Accordingly if he is wrong in his opinion, he is the person who is hurt, for he is the person who has been deceived; for if a man shall suppose the true conjunction to be false, it is not the conjunction which is hindered, but the man who has been deceived about it. If you proceed then from these opinions, you will be mild in temper to him who reviles you; for say on each occasion, It seemed so to him.
entries.reflection: Epictetus says that someone who treats you badly is doing what seems right to them. Say to yourself, it seemed so to him. It makes room for patience.
studyPrompts: Who treats you badly?
What might seem right to them?
How could patience change your response?

entries.passageText: Reflect, therefore, on this, that the effect of wisdom is a joy that is unbroken and continuous. The mind of the wise man is like the ultra-lunar firmament; eternal calm pervades that region. You have, then, a reason for wishing to be wise, if the wise man is never deprived of joy. This joy springs only from the knowledge that you possess the virtues. None but the brave, the just, the self-restrained, can rejoice.
entries.reflection: Seneca says wisdom brings a joy that is unbroken, like the calm above the clouds. Cheerfulness rooted in virtue does not depend on circumstances.
studyPrompts: What brings you steady joy?
What clouds your mood?
How could you share cheerfulness today?

entries.passageText: Retire into thyself. The rational principle which rules has this nature, that it is content with itself when it does what is just, and so secures tranquillity.
entries.reflection: Marcus says to retire into yourself; reason is content with itself when it acts justly. Solitude can be found within.
studyPrompts: Where do you find solitude?
What do you find when you turn inward?
How could you make time for it?

entries.passageText: In the gymnastic exercises suppose that a man has torn thee with his nails, and by dashing against thy head has inflicted a wound. Well, we neither show any signs of vexation, nor are we offended, nor do we suspect him afterwards as a treacherous fellow; and yet we are on our guard against him, not however as an enemy, nor yet with suspicion, but we quietly get out of his way. Something like this let thy behavior be in all the other parts of life; let us overlook many things in those who are like antagonists in the gymnasium. For it is in our power, as I said, to get out of the way, and to have no suspicion nor hatred.
entries.reflection: Marcus says that when someone scratches you in a wrestling match, you do not hold it against them; you just keep clear. Many quarrels can be let go the same way.
studyPrompts: What quarrel could you let go?
Whom do you suspect without need?
What would moving on look like?

entries.passageText: What need is there of suspicious fear, since it is in thy power to inquire what ought to be done? And if thou seest clear, go by this way content, without turning back; but if thou dost not see clear, stop and take the best advisers. But if any other things oppose thee, go on according to thy powers with due consideration, keeping to that which appears to be just. For it is best to reach this object, and if thou dost fail, let thy failure be in attempting this. He who follows reason in all things is both tranquil and active at the same time, and also cheerful and collected.
entries.reflection: Marcus says that if you see the way clearly, go on; if not, stop and take the best advisers; and if you fail, let it be in attempting what is right. Courage includes asking for counsel.
studyPrompts: What danger or challenge are you facing?
Do you see the way clearly?
Whose counsel could you seek?

entries.passageText: Remember that to change thy opinion and to follow him who corrects thy error is as consistent with freedom as it is to persist in thy error. For it is thy own, the activity which is exerted according to thy own movement and judgment, and indeed according to thy own understanding too.
entries.reflection: Marcus says changing your mind when someone corrects you is as much an act of freedom as holding firm. Accepting correction is your own choice.
studyPrompts: What criticism have you received?
Is it worth accepting?
How could you respond freely?

entries.passageText: Philosophy is no trick to catch the public; it is not devised for show. It is a matter, not of words, but of facts. It is not pursued in order that the day may yield some amusement before it is spent, or that our leisure may be relieved of a tedium that irks us. It moulds and constructs the soul; it orders our life, guides our conduct, shows us what we should do and what we should leave undone; it sits at the helm and directs our course as we waver amid uncertainties. Without it, no one can live fearlessly or in peace of mind. Countless things that happen every hour call for advice; and such advice is to be sought in philosophy.
entries.reflection: Seneca says philosophy is not for show; it shapes the soul, orders life and guides conduct. Real study changes how you live.
studyPrompts: What are you studying?
How is it changing you?
What would you like to understand better?

entries.passageText: When will it be your lot to attain this joy? Thus far, you have indeed not been sluggish, but you must quicken your pace. Much toil remains; to confront it, you must yourself lavish all your waking hours, and all your efforts, if you wish the result to be accomplished. This matter cannot be delegated to someone else.
entries.reflection: Seneca tells Lucilius he has not been sluggish, but must quicken his pace, because the work cannot be delegated. In dry seasons, keep putting in the effort.
studyPrompts: Where do you feel stalled?
What effort can only you make?
What small step could you take today?

entries.passageText: Remember how long thou hast been putting off these things, and how often thou hast received an opportunity from the gods, and yet dost not use it. Thou must now at last perceive of what universe thou art a part, and of what administrator of the universe thy existence is an efflux, and that a limit of time is fixed for thee, which if thou dost not use for clearing away the clouds from thy mind, it will go and thou wilt go, and it will never return.
entries.reflection: Marcus reminds himself how long he has put things off, and that his time is limited. Initiative means using the opportunity now.
studyPrompts: What have you been putting off?
What opportunity is in front of you?
What could you start today?

entries.passageText: Disease is an impediment to the body, but not to the will, unless the will itself chooses. Lameness is an impediment to the leg, but not to the will. And add this reflection on the occasion of everything that happens; for you will find it an impediment to something else, but not to yourself.
entries.reflection: Epictetus says illness is an obstacle to the body but not to the will. Pain is real, but it does not have to command your choices. If pain is wearing you down, seek help.
studyPrompts: What pain are you living with?
What choices remain yours?
Who could help you with it?

entries.passageText: As thou thyself art a component part of a social system, so let every act of thine be a component part of social life. Whatever act of thine then has no reference either immediately or remotely to a social end, this tears asunder thy life, and does not allow it to be one, and it is of the nature of a mutiny, just as when in a popular assembly a man acting by himself stands apart from the general agreement.
entries.reflection: Marcus says every act should be part of social life; an act with no reference to the common good is like a mutiny. We live as members of a community.
studyPrompts: How do your actions affect your community?
Where are you acting alone?
What could you do for the common good?

entries.passageText: This is what I mean, Lucilius: a holy spirit indwells within us, one who marks our good and bad deeds, and is our guardian. As we treat this spirit, so are we treated by it. Indeed, no man can be good without the help of God. Can one rise superior to fortune unless God helps him to rise? He it is that gives noble and upright counsel. In each good man A god doth dwell, but what god know we not.
entries.reflection: Seneca says a holy spirit dwells within us, marking our good and bad deeds and acting as our guardian. For him, reverence starts inside.
studyPrompts: What do you hold sacred?
What inner guide do you listen to?
How could you show reverence today?

entries.passageText: To the jaundiced honey tastes bitter, and to those bitten by mad dogs water causes fear; and to little children the ball is a fine thing. Why then am I angry? Dost thou think that a false opinion has less power than the bile in the jaundiced or the poison in him who is bitten by a mad dog?
entries.reflection: Marcus notes that honey tastes bitter to the jaundiced. When anger makes everything taste bitter, the problem may be in our view, not the world.
studyPrompts: What tastes bitter to you right now?
Could your view be part of it?
What would sweeten it?

entries.passageText: When thou art offended at any man's fault, forthwith turn to thyself and reflect in what like manner thou dost err thyself; for example, in thinking that money is a good thing, or pleasure, or a bit of reputation, and the like. For by attending to this thou wilt quickly forget thy anger, if this consideration also is added, that the man is compelled: for what else could he do? or, if thou art able, take away from him the compulsion.
entries.reflection: Marcus says that when someone's fault offends you, first turn to yourself and ask how you err in a similar way. Self-examination makes correction gentler.
studyPrompts: Whose fault offends you?
How do you err in similar ways?
How could you correct more gently?

entries.passageText: Meanwhile, I owe you my little daily contribution; you shall be told what pleased me to-day in the writings of Hecato; it is these words: “What progress, you ask, have I made? I have begun to be a friend to myself.” That was indeed a great benefit; such a person can never be alone. You may be sure that such a man is a friend to all mankind. Farewell.
entries.reflection: Seneca shares his daily thought from Hecato: I have begun to be a friend to myself. A small daily practice can lead to real progress.
studyPrompts: What daily practice do you keep?
Are you a friend to yourself?
What small habit could you add?

entries.passageText: I am grieved to hear that your friend Flaccus is dead, but I would not have you sorrow more than is fitting. That you should not mourn at all I shall hardly dare to insist; and yet I know that it is the better way. But what man will ever be so blessed with that ideal steadfastness of soul, unless he has already risen far above the reach of Fortune? Even such a man will be stung by an event like this, but it will be only a sting. We, however, may be forgiven for bursting into tears, if only our tears have not flowed to excess, and if we have checked them by our own efforts. Let not the eyes be dry when we have lost a friend, nor let them overflow. We may weep, but we must not wail.
entries.reflection: Seneca writes to a grieving friend: we may weep, but we must not wail; let not the eyes be dry, nor overflow. Grief is natural and should be allowed.
studyPrompts: What are you grieving?
Have you allowed yourself to grieve?
Who could you grieve with?

entries.passageText: It is thy duty to order thy life well in every single act; and if every act does its duty as far as is possible, be content; and no one is able to hinder thee so that each act shall not do its duty.--But something external will stand in the way. Nothing will stand in the way of thy acting justly and soberly and considerately.--But perhaps some other active power will be hindered. Well, but by acquiescing in the hindrance and by being content to transfer thy efforts to that which is allowed, another opportunity of action is immediately put before thee in place of that which was hindered, and one which will adapt itself to this ordering of which we are speaking.
entries.reflection: Marcus says that when something blocks one action, accept it and turn to what is allowed; another opportunity is put before you. Adaptability turns obstacles into new paths.
studyPrompts: What is blocking you?
What is still allowed?
What new opportunity might be in front of you?

entries.passageText: Look round at the courses of the stars, as if thou wert going along with them; and constantly consider the changes of the elements into one another, for such thoughts purge away the filth of the terrene life.
entries.reflection: Marcus says to look at the courses of the stars as if you were moving with them; such thoughts clear the mind. The night sky lifts us beyond daily cares.
studyPrompts: When did you last look at the stars?
What cares do they put in perspective?
What clears your mind?

entries.passageText: When you have decided that a thing ought to be done, and are doing it, never avoid being seen doing it, though the many shall form an unfavorable opinion about it. For if it is not right to do it, avoid doing the thing; but if it is right, why are you afraid of those who shall find fault wrongly?
entries.reflection: Epictetus says that once you decide something is right, do not hide while doing it, even if many disapprove. Conscience gives you courage.
studyPrompts: What do you know is right?
Are you hiding it?
What would acting openly look like?

entries.passageText: Take away thy opinion, and then there is taken away the complaint, "I have been harmed." Take away the complaint, "I have been harmed," and the harm is taken away.
entries.reflection: Marcus says take away the opinion, I have been harmed, and the harm goes with it. Self-pity often grows from the story we tell.
studyPrompts: What story are you telling about your harm?
What would change if you set it aside?
Who could help you see it differently?

entries.passageText: But just as we take on faith such estimates of values, so let us take on the faith of the people this truth, that nothing is more honourable than a grateful heart. This phrase will be echoed by all cities, and by all races, even those from savage countries. Upon this point good and bad will agree.
entries.reflection: Seneca says that all peoples agree nothing is more honorable than a grateful heart. Gratitude is universal.
studyPrompts: Whom are you grateful to?
How could you show it?
What gratitude have you received?

entries.passageText: To-day has been unbroken; no one has filched the slightest part of it from me. The whole time has been divided between rest and reading. A brief space has been given over to bodily exercise, and on this ground I can thank old age—my exercise costs very little effort; as soon as I stir, I am tired. And weariness is the aim and end of exercise, no matter how strong one is.
entries.reflection: Seneca describes his day in old age: unbroken time for rest and reading, and a little exercise. Aging can bring its own peace and freedom.
studyPrompts: How do you feel about growing older?
What would a good day in old age look like?
What do you want to keep doing?

entries.passageText: Do not have such an opinion of things as he has who does thee wrong, or such as he wishes thee to have, but look at them as they are in truth.
entries.reflection: Marcus says not to see things as the person who wrongs you sees them, or as they want you to, but as they truly are. Truth frees us from others' distortions.
studyPrompts: Whose view are you adopting?
What is the truth of the situation?
How could you see more clearly?

entries.passageText: As it happens to thee in the amphitheatre and such places, that the continual sight of the same things, and the uniformity, make the spectacle wearisome, so it is in the whole of life; for all things above, below, are the same and from the same. How long then?
entries.reflection: Marcus compares the sameness of life to a long show at the amphitheatre that grows tedious. Naming boredom honestly is a first step toward finding fresh purpose.
studyPrompts: Where do you feel bored?
What purpose could you bring to routine?
What could you notice afresh?

entries.passageText: It shows much more courage to remain dry and sober when the mob is drunk and vomiting; but it shows greater self-control to refuse to withdraw oneself and to do what the crowd does, but in a different way,—thus neither making oneself conspicuous nor becoming one of the crowd. For one may keep holiday without extravagance.
entries.reflection: Seneca says it takes self-control to join a festival without excess, neither standing apart nor losing yourself in the crowd. You can celebrate with moderation.
studyPrompts: How do you celebrate?
Where do you go too far?
What would joyful moderation look like?

entries.passageText: How cruel it is not to allow men to strive After the things which appear to them to be suitable to their nature and profitable! And yet in a manner thou dost not allow them to do this, when thou art vexed because they do wrong. For they are certainly moved towards things because they suppose them to be suitable to their nature and profitable to them. But it is not so. Teach them then, and show them without being angry.
entries.reflection: Marcus says it is cruel not to let people pursue what seems good to them. Teach them if they are wrong, without anger.
studyPrompts: Whom do you struggle to tolerate?
What seems good to them?
How could you teach without anger?

entries.passageText: “But it is the fool,” you say, “who is inconsistent; nothing suits him for long.” But how or when can we tear ourselves away from this folly? No man by himself has sufficient strength to rise above it; he needs a helping hand, and some one to extricate him.
entries.reflection: Seneca says no one has the strength to rise out of it alone; we need a helping hand. That is true of despair too. If you are in despair, use Need to talk? in this app or speak to a chaplain today.
studyPrompts: What are you struggling with?
Who could be a helping hand?
Who could you talk to today?

entries.passageText: When at a small cost you are supplied with everything for the body, do not be proud of this; nor, if you drink water, say on every occasion, I drink water. But consider first how much more frugal the poor are than we, and how much more enduring of labor. And if you ever wish to exercise yourself in labor and endurance, do it for yourself, and not for others. Do not embrace statues; but if you are ever very thirsty, take a draught of cold water and spit it out, and tell no man.
entries.reflection: Epictetus says not to boast about frugality or endurance; if you train yourself, do it for yourself, not for show. Modesty keeps virtue private.
studyPrompts: What do you do for show?
What could you do quietly?
What does modesty look like for you?

entries.passageText: A man is indeed lazy and careless, my dear Lucilius, if he is reminded of a friend only by seeing some landscape which stirs the memory; and yet there are times when the old familiar haunts stir up a sense of loss that has been stored away in the soul, not bringing back dead memories, but rousing them from their dormant state, just as the sight of a lost friend’s favourite slave, or his cloak, or his house, renews the mourner’s grief, even though it has been softened by time. Now, lo and behold, Campania, and especially Naples and your beloved Pompeii, struck me, when I viewed them, with a wonderfully fresh sense of longing for you. You stand in full view before my eyes. I am on the point of parting from you. I see you choking down your tears and resisting without success the emotions that well up at the very moment when you try to check them. I seem to have lost you but a moment ago. For what is not “but a moment ago” when one begins to use the memory?
entries.reflection: Seneca writes that familiar places stir his longing for Lucilius, and he recalls their parting and the tears held back. Departures stay with us.
studyPrompts: What parting do you remember?
How do you carry those you have left?
How could you say goodbye well?

entries.passageText: From Antisthenes: It is royal to do good and to be abused.
entries.reflection: Marcus quotes Antisthenes: it is royal to do good and be spoken ill of. Those with power should do good regardless of praise.
studyPrompts: What power do you have?
Do you do good even when criticized?
How could you use your position well?

entries.passageText: If a thing is in thy own power, why dost thou do it? but if it is in the power of another, whom dost thou blame,--the atoms [chance] or the gods? Both are foolish. Thou must blame nobody. For if thou canst, correct [that which is the cause]; but if thou canst not do this, correct at least the thing itself; but if thou canst not do even this, of what use is it to thee to find fault? for nothing should be done without a purpose.
entries.reflection: Marcus says that if something is in your power, do it; if not, blame no one; and if you can correct it, do. Frustration wastes energy on blame.
studyPrompts: What frustrates you?
Is it in your power?
What could you do instead of blaming?

entries.passageText: Everywhere and at all times it is in thy power piously to acquiesce in thy present condition, and to behave, justly to those who are about thee, and to exert thy skill upon thy present thoughts, that nothing shall steal into them without being well examined.
entries.reflection: Marcus says it is always in your power to accept your present condition, to act justly toward those around you, and to examine your thoughts. Acceptance is active.
studyPrompts: What are you struggling to accept?
How could you act justly within it?
What thoughts need examining?

entries.passageText: In the writings of the [Ephesians] there was this precept, constantly to think of some one of the men of former times who practiced virtue.
entries.reflection: Marcus records the precept to keep in mind someone from the past who practised virtue. Good examples can shape good habits.
studyPrompts: Whose example do you keep in mind?
What habit do they inspire?
How could you keep their example close?

entries.passageText: Love that only which happens to thee and is spun with the thread of thy destiny. For what is more suitable?
entries.reflection: Marcus says to love only what happens to you and is spun with your destiny. Accepting what comes can soften disappointment.
studyPrompts: What disappointed you?
What would accepting it look like?
What good could still come from it?

entries.passageText: And you too shall be shaded by the tree which Is slow to grow, but bringeth shade to cheer Your grandsons in the far-off years, as our poet Vergil says. Vergil sought, however, not what was nearest to the truth, but what was most appropriate, and aimed, not to teach the farmer, but to please the reader.
entries.reflection: Seneca quotes Vergil on planting trees that will shade one's grandsons. A legacy is what we plant for those after us.
studyPrompts: What are you planting for the future?
Who will benefit from your work?
What legacy were you given?

entries.passageText: If thou workest at that which is before thee, following right reason seriously, vigorously, calmly, without allowing anything else to distract thee, but keeping thy divine part pure, as if thou shouldst be bound to give it back immediately; if thou holdest to this, expecting nothing, fearing nothing, but satisfied with thy present activity according to nature, and with heroic truth in every word and sound which thou utterest, thou wilt live happy. And there is no man who is able to prevent this.
entries.reflection: Marcus says that if you work at what is before you seriously, vigorously and calmly, expecting and fearing nothing, you will live happily. Wholeheartedness brings peace.
studyPrompts: What are you working on?
Are you giving it your whole attention?
What distracts you?

entries.passageText: Judging by what you write me, and by what I hear, I am forming a good opinion regarding your future. You do not run hither and thither and distract yourself by changing your abode; for such restlessness is the sign of a disordered spirit. The primary indication, to my thinking, of a well-ordered mind is a man’s ability to remain in one place and linger in his own company.
entries.reflection: Seneca says restlessness is a sign of a disordered spirit; a well-ordered mind can stay in one place and be good company for itself.
studyPrompts: What makes you restless?
Can you be good company for yourself?
What would staying put look like?

entries.passageText: Say nothing more to thyself than what the first appearances report. Suppose that it has been reported to thee that a certain person speaks ill of thee. This has been reported; but that thou hast been injured, that has not been reported. I see that my child is sick. I do see; but that he is in danger, I do not see. Thus then always abide by the first appearances, and add nothing thyself from within, and then nothing happens to thee. Or rather add something like a man who knows everything that happens in the world.
entries.reflection: Marcus says to tell yourself no more than the first impressions report: someone speaks ill of you, not that you are harmed. Adding stories makes things heavier. If it is too much, ask for help.
studyPrompts: What is overwhelming you?
What are the facts, and what are you adding?
Who could help you?

entries.passageText: Our philosopher will therefore acknowledge that he owes a large debt to the ruler who makes it possible, by his management and foresight, for him to enjoy rich leisure, control of his own time, and a tranquillity uninterrupted by public employments. Shepherd! a god this leisure gave to me, For he shall be my god eternally.
entries.reflection: Seneca says the philosopher owes thanks to the ruler whose good management gives him peace and leisure. Good authority deserves gratitude.
studyPrompts: Who in authority has made your life better?
How could you thank them?
What does good leadership give others?

entries.passageText: In like manner you should rebuke these two kinds of men,—both those who always lack repose, and those who are always in repose. For love of bustle is not industry,—it is only the restlessness of a hunted mind. And true repose does not consist in condemning all motion as merely vexation; that kind of repose is slackness and inertia.
entries.reflection: Seneca warns against both constant bustle and constant idleness. Busyness is not industry, and true rest is not inertia.
studyPrompts: Are you too busy or too idle?
What does true rest look like for you?
How could you find balance?

entries.passageText: I therefore wish to impart to you this sudden change in myself; I should then begin to place a surer trust in our friendship,—the true friendship which hope and fear and self-interest cannot sever, the friendship in which and for the sake of which men meet death.
entries.reflection: Seneca speaks of true friendship that hope, fear and self-interest cannot break, a bond for which people have given their lives. Such friendship asks something of us.
studyPrompts: What friendships would you sacrifice for?
What does friendship ask of you?
How could you strengthen a bond?

entries.passageText: In discourse thou must attend to what is said, and in every movement thou must observe what is doing. And in the one thou shouldst see immediately to what end it refers, but in the other watch carefully what is the thing signified.
entries.reflection: Marcus says to attend to what is said in conversation and to what is done in every action. Attention is a form of respect.
studyPrompts: How well do you listen?
What do you miss when distracted?
How could you pay closer attention today?

entries.passageText: The measure of possession (property) is to every man the body, as the foot is of the shoe. If then you stand on this rule (the demands of the body), you will maintain the measure; but if you pass beyond it, you must then of necessity be hurried as it were down a precipice. As also in the matter of the shoe, if you go beyond the (necessities of the) foot, the shoe is gilded, then of a purple color, then embroidered; for there is no limit to that which has once passed the true measure.
entries.reflection: Epictetus says the body is the measure of what we own, as the foot is of the shoe; beyond that, there is no limit. Balance means knowing what is enough.
studyPrompts: What do you have beyond what you need?
Where have you lost balance?
What would enough look like?

entries.passageText: If you have assumed a character above your strength, you have both acted in this manner in an unbecoming way, and you have neglected that which you might have fulfilled.
entries.reflection: Epictetus warns that taking on a role beyond your strength means failing at it and neglecting the one you could have done. Ambition should fit your real abilities.
studyPrompts: What role are you aiming for?
Does it fit your strengths?
What role could you fill well now?

entries.passageText: That which does not make a man worse than he was, also does not make his life worse, nor does it harm him either from without or from within.
entries.reflection: Marcus says what does not make you worse does not harm your life. Your character is protected from many outside harms.
studyPrompts: What do you fear will harm you?
Could it make you worse as a person?
What inside you is safe?

entries.passageText: Try how the life of the good man suits thee, the life of him who is satisfied with his portion out of the whole, and satisfied with his own just acts and benevolent disposition.
entries.reflection: Marcus suggests trying the life of a good person, content with their own just acts and kindly disposition. Goodwill is a way of life to test.
studyPrompts: What would a day of goodwill look like?
Whom could you treat kindly?
How content are you with your own acts?

entries.passageText: Cast away opinion: thou art saved. Who then hinders thee from casting it away?
entries.reflection: Marcus says, cast away opinion and you are saved; who stops you? Much of what weighs on us can be put down.
studyPrompts: What opinion are you holding?
What would casting it away look like?
What stops you?

entries.passageText: The safety of life is this, to examine everything all through, what it is itself, that is its material, what the formal part; with all thy soul to do justice and to say the truth. What remains, except to enjoy life by joining one good thing to another so as not to leave even the smallest intervals between?
entries.reflection: Marcus says to do justice and speak truth with all your soul, and then enjoy life by joining one good thing to another. Life is meant to be lived fully. If you are struggling, reach out today.
studyPrompts: What makes you feel alive?
What good things could you join together today?
Who reminds you that your life matters?

entries.passageText: It is the month of December, and yet the city is at this very moment in a sweat. Licence is given to the general merrymaking. Everything resounds with mighty preparations,—as if the Saturnalia differed at all from the usual business day! So true it is that the difference is nil, that I regard as correct the remark of the man who said: “Once December was a month; now it is a year.”
entries.reflection: Seneca writes during the Saturnalia holiday that the whole city is busy celebrating. Holidays can feel strange when you are not where you expected to be.
studyPrompts: What holidays will you spend away?
How could you mark them where you are?
What makes a holiday meaningful?

entries.passageText: It is no evil for things to undergo change, and no good for things to subsist in consequence of change.
entries.reflection: Marcus says it is no evil for things to change. Change is natural, and transitions are part of life.
studyPrompts: What change are you facing?
What helps you accept change?
What might you gain from it?

entries.passageText: All things are implicated with one another, and the bond is holy; and there is hardly anything unconnected with any other thing. For things have been co-ordinated, and they combine to form the same universe [order]. For there is one universe made up of all things, and one god who pervades all things, and one substance, and one law, [one] common reason in all intelligent animals, and one truth; if indeed there is also one perfection for all animals which are of the same stock and participate in the reason.
entries.reflection: Marcus says all things are connected, and the bond between them is holy. We are joined by a common reason and purpose.
studyPrompts: Whom are you connected to?
How could you honor that bond?
What brings people together where you are?
